name: Reference Payments Platform (hand-authored CALM construct reference)
description: A small, internally-consistent fintech-shaped architecture, hand-authored to exercise every CALM 1.2 construct this project's research has confirmed against the real FINOS schema (see companion README.md for citations). NOT platform output — a teaching/reference document for improving pipeline/src/modules/calm-generator.

nodes.name: Cardholder
nodes.description: A customer initiating a card payment via the web/mobile client.

nodes.name: Payments Platform
nodes.description: Composite/boundary node for the whole logical system — the top-level node this project's own research names as the fix for 'no top-level application node' (node-type: system, composed-of below).

nodes.name: Payments Kubernetes Cluster
nodes.description: Runtime placement boundary — distinct from platform-system above: this models WHERE things run, not the logical domain grouping.

security.description: Security requirements for the Kubernetes cluster (reused verbatim from FINOS's own real published example — see README.md).

nodes.name: PCI DSS Cardholder Data Environment
nodes.description: A third, orthogonal boundary — not the logical domain (platform-system) or the runtime cluster (k8s-cluster), but the actual PCI DSS compliance scope: which nodes store, process, or transmit raw cardholder data. This is a real architectural fact for a payment platform specifically, not a generic construct-coverage addition.

pci-dss-scope-001.description: This node's composed-of set below IS this platform's PCI DSS scope declaration — everything else in the architecture is out of scope because it never receives raw cardholder data.

config.scope-rationale: notification-service and settlement-events only ever see a post-authorization outcome event (settlement.completed), never the raw PAN — standard PCI segmentation. Note this scope is LARGER than a well-architected payment platform would want: without a tokenizing PSP/hosted-fields boundary (deliberately out of scope for this reference — see README.md), checkout-webapp and api-gateway are both in-scope because raw card data genuinely passes through them, not because of a modeling shortcut.

nodes.name: Checkout Web App
nodes.description: The actual presentation layer the cardholder uses — collects card details client-side and submits them to the API gateway. Added deliberately: the earlier version of this example had 'end-user' interacting directly with 'api-gateway', which skips the presentation layer entirely and is not true of any real payment platform. Statically hosted (CDN/S3-shaped), not cluster-deployed — see k8s-deployed-in below.

nodes.name: API Gateway
nodes.description: Edge ingress — TLS termination and routing into the payments domain. No business logic of its own.

nodes.name: Payments Service
nodes.description: JAX-RS resource at /v1/payments (PaymentsApiResource) — creates payments, persists them, and publishes settlement events. Method-level @PreAuthorize on the write path.

security-rbac-001.description: Role-Based Access Control via Spring/Jakarta @PreAuthorize on the payment-creation path.

nodes.name: Notification Service
nodes.description: Consumes settlement.completed and emails a receipt. No HTTP surface of its own — pure event consumer, same shape as a real no-route control-bearing service this project has found in practice.

nodes.name: Payments Database
nodes.description: Managed PostgreSQL (JPA @Entity Payment mapped to table payments). Runs outside the Kubernetes cluster as a managed cloud service — deliberately NOT deployed-in k8s-cluster below.

nodes.name: settlement.completed topic
nodes.description: Kafka topic carrying settlement-completed events between the payments and notification domains.

relationships.description: Cardholder opens the checkout page and submits payment details.
Checkout web app submits the payment request to the API gateway.
Gateway routes authenticated requests to the Payments Service.

security.description: Security Controls for the connection (reused verbatim from FINOS's own real published example — see README.md).

relationships.description: Payments Service persists and reads payment records.
Payments Service publishes to settlement.completed via KafkaTemplate.send after a successful payment.
Notification Service consumes settlement.completed via @KafkaListener and sends a receipt email.
Logical domain composition: the payments platform is composed of these units (excludes the actor, which is external to the system).

Runtime placement: these three services run inside the Kubernetes cluster. checkout-webapp is deliberately excluded (statically hosted via CDN, not cluster-deployed — same class of exclusion as payments-db/settlement-events, now with a third, differently-shaped example: static frontend hosting rather than a managed backend service), payments-db is deliberately excluded (managed RDS, not cluster-hosted), and settlement-events is deliberately excluded (managed Kafka, not cluster-hosted) — composed-of above says what belongs to the domain, deployed-in here says only where a subset of it actually runs.

PCI DSS scope declaration: exactly the nodes that store, process, or transmit raw cardholder data. A third, independent composed-of relationship pointing at a different subset of the same node set than platform-composed-of above — proving composed-of isn't limited to one grouping per architecture.

flows.name: Process Card Payment
flows.description: End-to-end business flow from cardholder request through settlement notification.

transitions.description: Cardholder opens checkout and submits payment details.
Web app submits the payment request to the gateway.

security-rbac-001.description: Flow-level control — the fourth control-attachment level (architecture/node/relationship/flow), confirmed by calm.finos.org's own intermediate tutorial. This flow as a whole must be traceable to an authenticated, authorized initiator end-to-end, not just at the individual gateway hop.

security.description: Organization-wide network segmentation control requirements applicable to the whole architecture, not scoped to a single node or relationship (document-root controls — a real, distinct CALM construct from node-level and relationship-level controls above; reuses the same real FINOS example pair for a proven-valid URL).

metadata.value: Hand-authored construct-coverage reference for improving pipeline/src/modules/calm-generator — not a generated artefact, not gold for any coe-lab package.
Illustrative only: node/relationship counts, evidence file:line refs, and hostnames are invented for teaching purposes, not derived from a real scanned codebase.

nodes[].ownership on payments-service/payments-db is governed by an illustrative org standard, standards/company-node-standard.json (a JSON Schema extending core.json#/defs/node via allOf with {costCenter, owner}), enforced by patterns/company-base-pattern.json — see README.md §4.3 and §8. Actually run: `calm validate -p patterns/company-base-pattern.json -a architecture.calm.json -u url-mapping.json` correctly fails on the 8 nodes that lack ownership (end-user, checkout-webapp, api-gateway, notification-service, settlement-events, platform-system, k8s-cluster, pci-cde) and passes on these 2.
